title: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
summary: The permitting bill could make it easier to build data centers for A.I. but a novel provision would also force data centers to pay much more for power.

Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a[sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/climate/congress-energy-permitting-reform-vote.html) that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities.


The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers.


But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers.


The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and[triggering anger in many communities](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/01/us/politics/liberals-conservatives-data-centers.html) . Voters this month approved[at least 40 local ballot initiatives](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/technology/midterm-elections-ai-data-centers.html) to restrict the facilities.


Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill[have cast it as a boon to tech companies,](https://earthjustice.org/feature/bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-2026-impact-guide#data-centers) arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing.


By contrast, supporters have framed the bill as an opportunity to get tough on A.I. firms.


“The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” said Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and a co-author of the bill. “Data centers now have to pay for the extra costs that they bring to the grid when they come online. They do not get to have all that extra cost dumped out onto the utility’s rate base and picked up by all of the other ratepayers.”
